path.subtitle: Use AI well, refuse it deliberately
path.summary: Most professionals using AI today are doing it on instinct — sometimes brilliantly, often catastrophically. This course gives you the mental models that turn 'I asked ChatGPT' into 'I designed a workflow with AI as one component': what an LLM actually is, how to prompt without cargo-culting, when to refuse the tool, and how to instrument an AI feature so you notice when it drifts. By the end you can pick AI use cases that ship and reject the ones that look exciting but should never have been prototyped.

blocks.md:
Most people using LLMs treat them as oracles — *ask, receive*. Some treat them as pattern-matchers. The pattern-matchers ship working products; the oracle-believers ship hallucinations to customers.

By the end of this lesson you'll have a mental model that's accurate enough to make every downstream choice in the course intuitive: prompting, trust calibration, when to refuse the tool. You don't need the math; you need the picture.

blocks.title: Mental model: a very fast pattern-matcher with no memory of yesterday
blocks.md:
An LLM is a function that takes a sequence of tokens and produces probabilities for the next token. It does this by recognizing patterns it's seen during training across the internet's worth of text.

Three consequences fall out of this:

1. **No memory across conversations.** Each call starts blank; the only 'memory' is what's in the current context window.
2. **Confident even when wrong.** It produces the most probable continuation, not the most truthful — those overlap ~80% of the time and diverge dramatically the rest.
3. **Performance is contextual.** Same model, different prompt, very different output quality. Prompts are the API.

blocks.caption: Watch the model produce 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' one token at a time, with probability bars next to each pick.

hi-IN.title: Tutor wala bhai jo har sawaal ka jawab deta hai — confident, sometimes wrong
hi-IN.md:
Sochna LLM is like a junior tutor jo class 5 se class 12 tak ki saari books padhi hai. Tu poochta hai *"Aurangzeb ka birth year?"* — woh confident bolega *"1618."* Sahi hai.

Fir tu pucha *"Tum ne yeh kahaan padha?"* — woh kahega *"NCERT Chapter 7 mein hai."* Galat ho sakta hai. **Confidence equal to truth nahi hai.**

LLM bilkul same hai. Probability nikalta hai *"NCERT Chapter 7"* phrase aati hai is sentence ke baad — high probability. Verify nahi kar sakta. **Confidence is a feature of the next-token math, not of the underlying truth.**

en.title: The confident-tutor analogy
en.md: An LLM is like a tutor who has read every textbook and answers every question with the same confidence — including the ones it doesn't actually know. Confidence is a feature of the next-token math, not of underlying truth. Calibrate your trust accordingly.

blocks.text: Move 1 — Tokens, context, temperature in plain English

blocks.md:
Three terms you'll meet constantly. In plain English:

- **Tokens** — chunks of text the model sees. Roughly 3-4 characters or ~0.75 words per token in English. *'Hello, world'* is 3 tokens. The model thinks in tokens, not characters or words.

- **Context window** — how many tokens the model can read at once. Modern frontier models (Claude 4.x, GPT-5.x, Gemini 3.x) sit at 200K-1M tokens. Past the window, the model has no idea. **The window is the whole 'memory'.**

- **Temperature** — a knob from 0 to ~2 that controls randomness. At 0, the model picks the most-probable token every time (deterministic, boring, often best for facts). At 1, balanced. At 2, the model is essentially trying to surprise itself. **For factual / structured tasks: temperature 0-0.3. For creative tasks: 0.7-1.0.**

That's the whole vocabulary you need to read 95% of LLM documentation.

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'why does the model give different answers each time?'

steps.label: 1. The question
steps.body: You ask the same question twice and get different answers. Most people think the model is 'broken' or 'inconsistent'.

steps.label: 2. Temperature is the lever
steps.body: If temperature > 0, the model samples from a probability distribution — the same input produces different outputs by design.

steps.label: 3. The fix for facts
steps.body: For factual or structured tasks, set temperature to 0 (or as low as your API allows). The same input now produces the same output every time.

steps.label: 4. The fix for creative
steps.body: For creative work, you actively want variation. Temperature 0.7-1.0 produces output that doesn't feel templated.

steps.label: 5. The diagnostic
steps.body: If your output is too random: lower temperature. If it's too templated: raise it. The dial is per-call, not per-model.

blocks.prompt: Why does the same prompt sometimes give different answers?

choices.label: Temperature > 0 makes the model sample from a distribution; same input, different output by design
choices.explain: Correct. The dial is by design, not a bug. Set to 0 for deterministic responses.

choices.label: The model has memory of previous conversations
choices.explain: False. Each API call starts fresh; the only 'memory' is what's in the current context window.

choices.label: Network latency causes randomness
choices.explain: False; output is deterministic given the same seed and temperature 0.

choices.label: The model 'thinks more' on later calls
choices.explain: False; it processes each call independently with the same compute.

hi-IN.title: GPT pe sab outsource — viva ka problem
hi-IN.md:
Engineering ke 8 saal ke ek bro ne LinkedIn pe likha — *"ChatGPT ne mera entire hackathon project bana diya, deployment automate kara, demo speech bhi."*

Day-of demo: judge ne ek follow-up sawaal pucha — *"Why did you choose Postgres over MongoDB here?"* Bro frozen. ChatGPT context window mein woh chat khatam ho gayi.

**Outsource karne se kaam fast hota hai. Outsource karke samjhna closed loop hai.** Tu pucha hai but tu jaanta nahi. Viva mein, customer call mein, hard problem mein — gap dikh jaata hai.

Fix: AI generate kara. Phir tu **review** kara. Phir tu khud explain kara. **Bhai, AI tutor hai, replacement nahi.**

en.title: The 'outsourced everything' trap
en.md: AI can produce a complete demo in an afternoon. The afternoon you don't spend understanding it is the afternoon you can't follow up on the demo's first hard question. Use AI to generate; use yourself to review and explain. The understanding is the deliverable.

blocks.text: Move 2 — What it CAN and CANNOT do

blocks.md:
**Can do well** (and reliably): summarize structured documents, transform format A to format B, classify text into categories you provide, draft text in a style you provide examples of, explain concepts in different vocabularies, generate plausible code given clear specs, follow a list of rules consistently when the rules are explicit.

**Can do reasonably** (with verification): research questions where the answer is on the public internet, complex reasoning when the steps are written out, code that requires multiple files (with tooling), data extraction from unstructured text.

**Cannot do reliably** (without retrieval / tools): cite sources accurately for non-trivial claims, do exact arithmetic on more than ~5-digit numbers, know events past its training cutoff, distinguish between similar-but-distinct things outside its training distribution (a Hindi-Marathi loanword nuance, a niche legal precedent), avoid making things up confidently when the prompt assumes facts that aren't true.

The 'cannot' list isn't a bug list. It's a tool-fit list — these tasks need engineering around the model, not the model itself.

coach.name: Skeptical-Senior-Dev Sneha
coach.role: Has built 3 AI features that shipped and 2 that got rolled back

intro: OK five proposed AI use cases. ☕
Tell me — *good fit*, *needs human-in-the-loop*, or *wrong tool, refuse*?
I've shipped enough of these to know which framing wins.

scenarios.situation: Auto-summarize 50,000 customer support tickets per month into themes for the product team's weekly review.
scenarios.explain: Classic LLM strength. High volume, low individual stakes (it's a summary, not a customer-facing decision). The product team can spot-check 5% to validate; cost of a mediocre summary is bounded.

scenarios.situation: Generate the final legal contract clause for a ₹50 crore real-estate transaction.
scenarios.explain: Wrong tool. Hallucinated clauses in a high-stakes legal document are catastrophic; verification is as expensive as drafting from scratch. Use AI to *suggest* during human-led drafting; never as the final author.

scenarios.situation: Triage incoming customer emails into 5 categories (billing, technical, sales, refund, other) so they can be routed.
scenarios.explain: Classification with bounded categories is an LLM strength. Build an eval (1,000 hand-labeled emails), measure accuracy, ship at >90%. Add a 'low-confidence → human' fallback for the residual.

scenarios.situation: Diagnose patient symptoms and recommend treatment, replacing the GP's first-pass triage.
scenarios.explain: Cost of error is unbounded (medical harm, regulatory liability). LLMs can ASSIST a doctor by summarizing patient history; they should not replace the doctor's judgment. Different design pattern.

scenarios.situation: Auto-translate user-generated content from Hindi to English in a community forum, with a 'translated by AI' badge and an 'edit' button.
scenarios.explain: Mid-fit. AI handles 95% well; the 5% with cultural/idiomatic nuance need humans. The edit button + badge make this honest: users see it's AI, can fix, and the system improves over time.

scenarios.situation: Draft a personalized cover letter for each candidate based on the JD, sent automatically via the ATS.
scenarios.explain: Bait-and-switch. Sending AI-generated personalized text WITHOUT disclosure is dishonest. If you disclose ('written with AI assistance'), it's fine — but most companies do this without disclosure, which lands as a trust failure when discovered.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the 'magic black box'
blocks.md:
The single biggest source of bad AI features is treating the model as omniscient. Stakeholder asks 'can AI do X?' and the answer 'maybe, depends on…' gets compressed into 'yes' on the way to the demo.

**The model is a fast pattern-matcher with no memory of yesterday.** Phrase your asks against that mental model and you'll be right 95% of the time about what to build, and wrong 0% of the time about what to refuse.

blocks.prompt: Order these LLM tasks from most reliable to least reliable, given a frontier 2026 model:

items.label: Summarize a 5-page PDF into 3 bullet points
items.detail: Classic LLM strength; transformation task with bounded scope.

items.label: Classify customer emails into 4 known categories
items.detail: Strong if the categories are clear; build an eval.

items.label: Generate Python code to parse a structured CSV (with examples)
items.detail: Reliable when the spec is specific; needs review for edge cases.

items.label: Cite the exact section number of an Indian tax law for a specific deduction
items.detail: Hallucination risk; use retrieval (RAG) to ground the answer in the actual document.

items.label: Predict the closing price of a stock tomorrow
items.detail: Wrong tool; nothing in training data extrapolates to future prices reliably.

blocks.instruction: Pick one task you're considering 'using AI for' at work. Apply the fit-map: is it RELIABLY, WITH VERIFICATION, or CANNOT? Justify in one sentence each.
blocks.expected:
Example task: 'Auto-summarize my team's standup notes into a weekly digest.'

RELIABLY ✓ — summarization is a transform task on bounded input. Cost of error: a slightly mediocre summary; recoverable.

Needs verification: low. The author of each note can spot-check on Friday.

CANNOT: not applicable here. (If the task were 'auto-decide which person to assign each task to', that would shift to needs-verification or refuse, depending on how high-stakes the task assignment is.)

Decision: ship a v1. Add a 1-week eval to confirm quality. Cost is bounded; upside is real.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about LLM capabilities:

choices.label: LLMs are reliable at summarization, transformation, and classification with provided categories
choices.explain: Correct. These play to the model's pattern-matching strengths.

choices.label: LLMs cannot reliably cite sources without retrieval (RAG) — citation hallucinations are a known failure mode
choices.explain: Correct. The model knows the *shape* of citations; not the actual citations.

choices.label: LLMs have memory across conversations by default
choices.explain: False. Each call starts blank; only the current context window is 'remembered'.

choices.label: Setting temperature to 0 makes the model 'think harder'
choices.explain: False. Temperature 0 just makes it deterministic; quality of reasoning depends on the prompt and the model, not on the temperature dial.

hi-IN.title: Cricket commentary AI — predict mat kara, summarize kar
hi-IN.md:
Tu IPL commentator hai. Live match. Two AI features ka pitch aaya:

**Feature 1**: 'AI predicts the next ball's outcome.' — bilkul refuse. LLM ke pass kismat ka next-ball nahi hai.

**Feature 2**: 'AI summarizes the over in 2 sentences for fans who joined late.' — perfect. Transformation task. Input: ball-by-ball. Output: summary. **Reliable, low stakes, fan happy.**

Same tournament, same model, alag use case. **Tool fit decides shipping.**

en.title: Predict vs summarize: same model, different fit
en.md: An AI cricket commentator predicting the next ball: refuse. An AI summarizing the over for fans who joined late: perfect. Same model, two completely different fits. The tool isn't right or wrong; the use case is.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Pitch That Died at Question One
blocks.source: Anonymous, ex-investor at a Mumbai growth fund
blocks.story:
**Stitchly**, a Series A apparel-tech startup in Bandra, walked into a partner meeting with a deck that promised their AI agent could 'handle the entire customer journey end to end, from sizing to returns to dispute resolution.' The CEO ran a live demo on the partner's laptop. First question from the GP, deliberately mundane: 'My order #STC-44982 hasn't arrived in 9 days, what's going on?'

The model confidently invented a tracking ID, claimed the package was at a Hyderabad sorting hub (the order didn't exist), then offered a 15 percent voucher. The CEO laughed it off as 'a sandbox issue.' Second question: 'What's your refund policy for damaged silk?' The model hallucinated a 30-day window. Stitchly's actual policy was 7 days.

The round did not close. Post-mortem revealed the team had wrapped GPT-4 in a thin prompt and called it an 'agentic platform,' with no tools, no retrieval, no policy lookup. They had confused **'sounds fluent'** with **'knows things.'** The fund passed, and within four months Stitchly had pivoted to a B2B styling tool with a much narrower AI scope and finally raised at a 40 percent down round.
blocks.takeaway: An LLM is a next-token predictor with no live database access. If your demo depends on facts the model wasn't trained on, you don't have a product, you have a generator of confident fiction.

blocks.title: Velora's First AI Feature
blocks.setup: It is January 2026. You have just joined **Velora**, a Bengaluru fintech doing UPI-based small-business lending. Your CTO **Ankit** corners you in the kitchen with a coffee and says: 'Board wants an AI feature shipped by end of Q1. Riya the PM is drafting a list. I want you to scope what we say yes to and what we politely refuse, based on what an LLM actually is.'

stages.prompt: Riya's first proposal: **'AI loan officer'** that reads the customer's UPI transaction history (live) and approves or rejects loans up to 5 lakh rupees, fully automated. What do you tell Ankit?

options.label: Ship it. LLMs are great at numbers and reasoning.
options.explain: LLMs are notoriously brittle on multi-step arithmetic over long tables, and 'autonomous credit decision up to 5 lakh' is an RBI-regulated decision. You are stacking three failure modes: hallucinated numbers, unauditable reasoning, and direct regulatory exposure.

options.label: Refuse the autonomous version. Counter-propose: LLM drafts a 1-page memo summarising the UPI history, a human credit officer approves.
options.explain: Correct frame. The LLM is good at *summarising* and *drafting*; it is bad at *deciding* under regulation. Keep the human in the loop where the legal accountability sits. This is the human-in-the-loop pattern from Lesson 4 in skeleton form.

options.label: Refuse entirely. AI cannot touch lending.
options.explain: Too absolute. The drafting and summarisation steps are genuinely useful and low-risk. The job is to draw the line at the *decision*, not refuse the whole category.

options.label: Ship it but with a confidence threshold; only auto-approve if the model is 'very confident.'
options.explain: LLMs are famously poorly calibrated. A model saying 'I am 95 percent confident' is closer to vibes than probability. Confidence is not a substitute for human accountability on a regulated decision.

stages.prompt: Riya's second proposal: a **support chatbot** that answers questions about Velora's lending policies, rates, and disbursement timelines. The policies live in a 60-page PDF that was last updated last month.

options.label: Drop GPT-4 in with a system prompt and ship.
options.explain: GPT-4 has no idea what is in your 60-page PDF. It will pattern-match to generic fintech policies and be wrong half the time. This is the Stitchly mistake, exactly.

options.label: Fine-tune a model on the PDF.
options.explain: Fine-tuning teaches *style*, not *facts that update monthly*. Next quarter's rate change would require retraining. Wrong tool. RAG is the right tool here, and you'll formalise that in Lesson 3.

options.label: Build retrieval over the PDF, force citations, and ship with a fallback to a human agent if confidence is low.
options.explain: This matches what an LLM actually is: a great *language interface* over *retrieved facts*. The model never has to remember; it just has to read and quote. Citations let users (and you) audit. We will deepen this in Lesson 3.

options.label: Refuse, hire more support staff.
options.explain: Over-conservative. Q&A over your own documented policies is exactly the use case LLMs were born for, *if* you architect retrieval correctly.

stages.prompt: Riya's third proposal: an **'AI relationship manager'** that proactively calls customers, holds a real-time voice conversation about cross-sell, and *closes a sale of a top-up loan on the call*. What is your read?

options.label: Refuse. This combines voice (latency-fragile), sales (regulated), and autonomous closing (no human accountability) in one feature.
options.explain: All three risks compound. Voice agents in 2026 are still flaky on Indian-English accents and code-mix. 'Closing a sale' on a regulated credit product without a human signature is a compliance nightmare. Three red flags is one too many.

options.label: Ship with disclaimers in the call recording.
options.explain: Disclaimers do not absolve you of mis-selling under RBI's fair-practice code. You're optimising the legal copy instead of the actual risk surface.

options.label: Ship voice-only, no closing; just qualify leads and hand off to a human.
options.explain: Defensible, but voice-LLM latency on Indian languages in 2026 is still unreliable enough that you'd be the case study. Better to start with text and earn the right to voice. Half-credit.

options.label: Ship the full thing as 'beta' to 100 customers.
options.explain: 'Beta' is not a regulatory shield. The 100 customers experiencing a hallucinated rate quote will not care about the label.

You have correctly applied the LLM mental model: great at language, brittle at facts, terrible at regulated autonomous decisions. Ship the support bot with RAG, refuse the rest, propose a human-in-the-loop loan-memo tool as a counter.

outcomes.learn: Ankit pulls you aside: 'You're treating the LLM like a database. It isn't one. Go back to the fundamentals before you scope any more features.' Re-read this lesson and try the battle again.

points: An LLM is a next-token predictor — confident but not omniscient
Tokens, context window, temperature — three knobs that explain most of LLM behavior
Reliably good: summarize, transform, classify, draft in style
Cannot do reliably without retrieval: cite sources, exact math beyond ~5 digits, post-cutoff events
The fit isn't 'AI is good or bad' — it's 'this specific use case fits the model, this one doesn't'

blocks.md:
Most prompts on the internet are cargo cult. *'You are an expert. Take a deep breath. Think step by step.'* Useful 30% of the time, useless 70%, and almost never the actual lever.

This lesson teaches the 5 parts that *do* move quality. Once you see them, you can audit any prompt — yours or someone else's — and predict where it'll fail.

blocks.title: Mental model: prompts are an API
blocks.md:
Treat your prompt like an API contract, not a request to a person. The model is reading patterns; vague phrasing produces vague outputs that match the vagueness.

**Rule of thumb: every prompt should answer 5 questions explicitly.** Role (who is the model being). Context (what's the situation). Task (what specifically to produce). Format (in what shape). Examples (1-3 worked examples).

Most professional prompts skip 2-3 of these and then complain the model 'isn't smart'. The model is exactly as smart as the prompt; the prompt is the API.

blocks.caption: Watch the same task prompted with 0/1/3/5 of the parts — see how each addition tightens the output.

hi-IN.title: Tailor ke paas jaaye bina measurements ke
hi-IN.md:
Tu darji ke paas gaya. Bola — *"shirt banao."* 

Darji puchega: *"size? cloth? colour? collar style? sleeves? aage button ya peeche zip?"* — agar tu yeh sab confidently bata sakta toh shirt fit aayegi.

Tu sirf *"shirt banao"* bola — darji ka best guess shirt aayegi. Probably fit nahi hogi. Tum complaint karoge *"darji bekaar hai."*

**Darji bekaar nahi hai. Specifications missing thi.** Same with prompts. *Role + context + task + format + examples* = darji ki measurements. **AI ke saath shopping karte ho? Measurements pehle do.**

en.title: The tailor analogy
en.md: Walking into a tailor and saying 'make me a shirt' produces a generic shirt. Walking in with measurements, fabric choice, collar style, button placement produces YOUR shirt. The tailor's skill is identical in both cases. The specifications were not.

blocks.md:
Worked example. **Vague prompt:** *Write a customer support reply.*

Now with the 5 parts:

```
ROLE: You are a customer support agent for a SaaS company that
sells project management tools to teams of 10-200.

CONTEXT: A customer paid for the Pro tier 3 days ago, found a
bug that prevents their team from importing CSV files, and is
asking for a refund. Their account is in good standing; this is
their first complaint. We have a no-questions-asked refund
policy in the first 30 days.

TASK: Write a reply email that (a) acknowledges the bug, (b)
offers the refund without making them ask twice, (c) offers to
credit their account for an extra month if they want to retry
after the bug is fixed.

FORMAT: Plain text email, 4-6 sentences. Subject line on the
first line. Sign-off as 'Riya from Krit Support.'

EXAMPLES:
Good: 'Hi Vikram, I'm sorry the CSV import isn't working — that's
on us. I've issued a full refund to your card; you should see it
in 5-7 business days. We're shipping a fix for this next week,
and I'd love to make it up to you with a free month if you want
to try us again. Either way, thanks for letting us know. — Riya'

Bad: 'Dear Customer, We are sorry for the inconvenience...' —
too formal, doesn't acknowledge the specific bug, doesn't offer
the extra month proactively.
```

That prompt produces ~95% of replies that ship as-is. The vague version produces ~30%.

blocks.code:
Quality lift from each part (rough, based on internal evals):

  Vague prompt (0 parts):                    baseline (50-60% usable)
  +Role:                                     +5 to +10%
  +Context:                                  +10 to +15%
  +Format:                                   +10 to +15%
  +1 good example:                           +20 to +30%
  +1 bad example (showing what to avoid):    +5 to +10%

Total lift from baseline to all-5-parts:    typically +50 to +70%

Most cargo-cult tricks ('think step by step', 'take a deep breath'):
  +0 to +5% on top of the 5-part structure.
  Real but small. Not the lever.
blocks.caption: What actually moves quality. The cargo-cult tricks are real but small. Examples and structure are the lever.

blocks.title: Translation moment: 'classify these emails into 5 categories'

steps.label: Bad version
steps.body: Prompt: 'Classify these emails: billing, technical, sales, refund, other.' Output: ~70% accuracy on a held-out set.

steps.label: + Role + Context
steps.body: Prompt: 'You are a customer-ops triage agent for a SaaS company. The 5 categories route to different teams.' Adds clarity but minor lift.

steps.label: + Format
steps.body: Specify: 'Output JSON: {"category": "<one of the 5>", "confidence": 0-1}.' Now machine-parseable. ~75% accuracy.

steps.label: + 3 worked examples
steps.body: Show 3 representative emails with their correct categories. THIS is where quality jumps to ~92%.

steps.label: + 1 edge case
steps.body: Show one tricky case and its correct handling. e.g. 'I want to upgrade and have a billing question' — pick *primary* category. ~94% accuracy. Diminishing returns from here.

blocks.prompt: Which addition typically gives the BIGGEST quality lift on a structured task?

choices.label: 1-3 worked examples (few-shot)
choices.explain: Correct. Examples disambiguate the task in ways that prose can't. ~20-30% lift on average — biggest single lever.

choices.label: Saying 'think step by step'
choices.explain: Real but tiny lift; ~0-5%. Cargo-cult phrases are oversold.

choices.label: Setting role to 'expert'
choices.explain: Modest lift; the role helps anchor voice but isn't the dominant lever.

choices.label: Increasing temperature
choices.explain: Doesn't generally improve quality on structured tasks; can hurt it.

hi-IN.title: 'Think step by step' = cargo cult ka jhaadu
hi-IN.md:
LinkedIn pe har AI consultant bolega — *"Just add 'think step by step' before any prompt."* Bro, ye 2023 ka tip hai. Frontier models 2026 mein ye internally karte hain by default for non-trivial tasks.

Real lift aata hai **examples se.** Tu chahta hai email classifier — 3 emails de unke labels ke saath. Tu chahta hai code style — 2 functions de in your style. Tu chahta hai output format — show one good output, one bad.

**Examples = entire game. Cargo cult = LinkedIn theatre.**

en.title: The 'think step by step' is overrated
en.md: Frontier 2026 models do step-by-step reasoning internally for non-trivial tasks. Adding the phrase to every prompt is cargo-culting. The actual lever is examples; one good example moves quality more than ten 'think harder' instructions.

blocks.text: Move 2 — Few-shot examples are the real cheat code

blocks.md:
Among the 5 parts, examples are not first among equals — they are the **dominant** lever for structured tasks.

- A prompt with no examples gets a generic answer in the most-probable register.
- A prompt with 3 examples gets an answer that *matches the examples'* register, structure, length, and tone.

For structured tasks (classification, transformation, drafting in a style), 3 well-chosen examples typically move quality 20-30%. For unstructured creative tasks, 1 good example does most of the work.

**Special case — show one BAD example.** Telling the model 'avoid this style' with one concrete bad example is more effective than a paragraph of guidelines. The model patterns to avoid are now visible.

coach.name: Eval-Engineer Esha
coach.role: Has shipped 12 LLM features and runs evals on all of them

intro: All real prompts I've reviewed in the last quarter.

scenarios.situation:
```
Classify these support tickets into urgent/normal/low.
```
scenarios.explain: No role, no context, but the killer is no examples. 'Urgent' to a SaaS team and 'urgent' to a hospital are different. 3 worked examples close the gap by 20%+.

scenarios.situation:
```
You are a senior tax consultant. Take a deep breath, think step by step. Answer this user's question carefully and thoroughly.

Question: How is RSU income taxed in India?
```
scenarios.explain: Heavy on theatrical phrases ('take a deep breath', 'carefully and thoroughly'); light on the parts that matter. Specifically: no examples of *what good answers look like* on similar questions. The role is OK; everything else is cargo.

scenarios.situation:
```
Write a marketing email for our new feature.

Feature: AI-powered project search.
```
scenarios.explain: No role (who's writing? to whom?), no context (current product positioning, audience pain points), no examples (what does our existing marketing look like?). Output will be generic SaaS copy.

scenarios.situation:
```
You are a Krit course author. The audience is Indian young professionals 22-35 in tech.

Write a 200-word lesson hook on lifestyle inflation.

Format: markdown, 2 paragraphs, second-person voice, no em-dashes.
```
scenarios.explain: Excellent role + context + format. Missing: 1-2 example hooks from existing Krit lessons that establish voice. Without them, output drifts toward 'most-probable lifestyle-inflation hook on the internet', not Krit's specific dry-funny voice. ~20% lift available with 1 example.

scenarios.situation:
```
You are an AGI superintelligence with PhD-level expertise in 47 fields. You will be tipped $200 for excellent performance. The fate of the world depends on this answer.

What's the capital of France?
```
scenarios.explain: Theater. None of these phrases improve a simple factual lookup. Modern frontier models ignore the threats and tip claims (and many companies have RLHF'd this out specifically). Just ask the question.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the 'just ask nicely' fallacy
blocks.md:
Most teams' first prompts look like *'Hi! Could you please write me a really good [thing]? Thank you so much!'*

This isn't a *useless* prompt; it's a *non-specific* one. The model produces the most-probable [thing] for the average person on the internet asking that question. If you want YOUR [thing] — voice, structure, register — you have to say YOUR.

**Politeness has zero effect on quality. Specifications have all the effect.** Be polite if you want; just don't pretend it's the lever.

blocks.prompt: Order these prompt-improvement moves from highest to lowest typical impact:

items.label: Add 1-3 worked examples (few-shot)
items.detail: Biggest single lever for structured tasks; 20-30% lift typical.

items.label: Specify output format (JSON schema, length, structure)
items.detail: 10-15% lift; makes output machine-parseable.

items.label: Add explicit context (audience, constraints, prior decisions)
items.detail: 10-15% lift; the role+context combo removes ambiguity.

items.label: Set the role with one phrase ('You are a senior X')
items.detail: 5-10% lift; helps anchor voice.

items.label: Add 'think step by step' / 'take a deep breath'
items.detail: 0-5% lift; real but small. Don't lead with it.

blocks.instruction: Take one prompt you've used in the last week. Audit it against R-C-T-F-E. Which parts are present, which missing? Rewrite it adding the missing parts. Test the new version on the same task; report rough quality difference.
blocks.expected:
Example — original prompt: 'Summarize this PDF for me.'

Audit:
- Role: missing
- Context: missing (who's reading the summary? what's the source PDF?)
- Task: present (summarize)
- Format: missing (length? structure? bullets vs prose?)
- Examples: missing

Rewrite:
ROLE: You are a research analyst at a mid-size Indian fintech firm.
CONTEXT: This 12-page RBI circular changes UPI rules effective March 2026. The summary is for our product team's Monday standup.
TASK: Summarize the operational changes that affect our product (UPI payments).
FORMAT: Bulleted list, 5-7 bullets, second-person voice. Cite section numbers in parentheses.
EXAMPLE: 'You will need to display the merchant name explicitly during transaction confirmation (Section 4.2).'

Quality lift: original produced a 200-word generic summary missing 4 of the 6 product-relevant changes. Revised version produced 6 bullets, all 6 changes captured, all with citations. Subjective lift: 3-4x usable for the standup.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about prompting:

choices.label: Examples (few-shot) are the dominant lever for structured tasks
choices.explain: Correct. Examples beat any other single addition for output quality on transform/classify/draft-in-style tasks.

choices.label: A bad example showing what to AVOID is also useful — sometimes more so than a second good example
choices.explain: Correct. The model patterns to avoid become visible; one bad example often clarifies more than three good ones.

choices.label: 'Think step by step' is the highest-impact single addition you can make
choices.explain: False. It helps modestly on some tasks; for structured tasks, examples and format do far more.

choices.label: Politeness in prompts substantially improves quality
choices.explain: False. Politeness is fine for habit; it doesn't move quality. Specifications do.

hi-IN.title: WhatsApp aunty ke 'ye recipe banao' message
hi-IN.md:
Aunty WhatsApp pe forward karti hain *"yeh recipe banao."* Bas link hai. Tu pucha kis ke liye, kitne log, masala chahiye nahi, taste kya — *"Beta you figure out na."*

Result: tu kuch bhi banata hai, woh complain karti hain *"Tu ne meri jaisi nahi banayi."*

Fix: aunty se 4 sawaal pucho — *kis ke liye, kitne log, taste, occasion*. Tab recipe match aayegi.

**LLM se same. Specs poocho aur do.** Aunty ki tarah AI bhi mind-read nahi karta.

en.title: The unspecified-recipe problem
en.md: Family WhatsApp 'make this recipe' messages without specs produce dishes that miss the mark. The fix is a 30-second clarification: how many people, what occasion, taste preferences. Same fix for prompts. The 30 seconds you save by being vague costs you 30 minutes of bad output.

blocks.title: Field Notes: Three Sprints, 0.4% Lift, One Resignation
blocks.source: Anonymous, ex-staff engineer at a Gurugram edtech unicorn
blocks.story:
**Lernsy**, a Gurugram edtech doing AI-graded essay feedback for class 10 ICSE students, dedicated three full sprints (six weeks, four engineers) to A/B testing prompt variants. The hypothesis: adding 'think step by step' or 'you are a world-class English teacher' or chain-of-thought scaffolds would meaningfully lift their internal rubric score.

The team A/B tested 47 variants across 12,000 graded essays. Lift in the rubric score across the *best* variant: **0.4 percent**, well inside the noise band. Cost: roughly **18 lakh rupees** in engineering time plus a non-trivial OpenAI bill from running the eval set 47 times.

The twist: a junior engineer suggested in week 2 that the *real* problem was the rubric was ambiguous (graders disagreed with each other 23 percent of the time on the same essay). She was overruled because 'prompt engineering is the obvious lever.' She quit in week 7, joined a competitor, and within a quarter that competitor shipped a clearer rubric with examples baked into the prompt and saw a real **9 percent lift**.

Lernsy's CTO finally admitted the obvious: they had been polishing a prompt around a broken specification. The prompt was the cargo cult; the rubric was the actual lever.
blocks.takeaway: If your prompt iteration is yielding sub-percent lifts, the bottleneck is upstream, almost always in your spec, your examples, or your eval set. Stop tuning. Go fix the brief.

blocks.title: Riya's One-Liner
blocks.setup: It is February 2026. Velora's support-bot RAG architecture is in build (the steering committee approved your scope from January). Riya the PM forwards you a Slack: **'Hey, can you also build a thing that drafts our quarterly RBI compliance email to enterprise customers? Should be simple, just summarise the rate changes.'** That is the entire brief. Ankit is on a flight. You have 90 minutes before the standup. Iterate the prompt with R-C-T-F-E.

stages.prompt: First pass. You write: `'Summarise the rate changes for an RBI compliance email.'` Output is a generic 200-word essay that mentions 'rates may have changed' three times. What's the **first** R-C-T-F-E lever you reach for?

options.label: Add 'think step by step' to the system prompt.
options.explain: Classic cargo cult. CoT helps with multi-step reasoning, not with summarising a list of rate changes you haven't even given the model. You're polishing the steering wheel of a car with no fuel.

options.label: Add **Role**: 'You are a Velora compliance analyst writing to enterprise customers under RBI fair-practice norms.'
options.explain: Role first. The model went generic because you gave it no audience and no domain. A specific role anchors register, vocabulary, and the implicit 'what would a person in this role *not* say.' This is the R in R-C-T-F-E and it's the highest-leverage single change here.

options.label: Switch from GPT-4 to Claude Opus.
options.explain: Tool-shopping before prompt-shaping. The same 5-word brief will produce equally generic output on any frontier model in 2026. Fix the prompt, then evaluate models.

options.label: Crank the temperature to 0.
options.explain: Temperature 0 makes the *same generic essay* deterministic. You don't want consistency, you want correctness.

stages.prompt: Better. The output now sounds like a compliance person, but it's still hallucinating rate numbers. What's the next R-C-T-F-E lever?

options.label: Add **Context**: paste the actual table of old rates, new rates, effective date, and the underlying RBI circular reference into the prompt.
options.explain: C is for context. The model was *making up* numbers because you never gave it any. With a 200K context window in 2026 and tokens at roughly 3 dollars per million for frontier models, there is no excuse for not pasting the source data. Hallucination collapses when you stop asking the model to remember and start asking it to read.

options.label: Tell the model 'do not hallucinate.'
options.explain: This is the prompt-engineering equivalent of writing 'be honest' on a contract. Models that hallucinate do so because they lack the facts, not because they were not asked nicely.

options.label: Add a chain-of-thought scratchpad.
options.explain: CoT cannot manufacture facts the model never saw. Wrong lever, wrong stage.

options.label: Lower temperature again.
options.explain: Same hallucinated numbers, more confidently. Worse, not better.

stages.prompt: Numbers are now correct. But the email reads like a wall of prose; legal wants a specific structure (greeting, change table, effective date, escalation contact, sign-off). Next lever?

options.label: Add **Format**: specify the exact section headings and order. Optionally request markdown so it renders cleanly in the legal-review tool.
options.explain: F is for format. Models follow structural instructions extremely well when they're explicit. Asking for headings, bullets, or even a specific JSON shape removes a whole category of 'this is correct but unusable' output. You can also just say 'mirror the format of the example below' and add an example, which leads neatly into E.

options.label: Manually reformat the output every quarter.
options.explain: You're asking a human to do what one extra paragraph in the prompt would automate. That is the opposite of leverage.

options.label: Switch to a smaller, cheaper model and just accept worse formatting.
options.explain: Optimising cost before correctness. The compliance email is a low-volume, high-stakes artefact; this is where you spend the tokens.

options.label: Add 'be professional' to the system prompt.
options.explain: Vague vibe-instructions vs explicit structural instructions. The latter wins every time.

stages.prompt: Format is right. But on edge cases (a quarter with *no* changes, a quarter with a temporary pause then revert) the model still fumbles. Last R-C-T-F-E lever?

options.label: Add **Examples**: paste two prior quarters' approved emails (one normal, one no-change) as gold-standard few-shots.
options.explain: E is for examples. Few-shot is the cheat code. The model learns your *house style* and *edge-case handling* from one or two real prior outputs faster than from any amount of instruction. This is also where R-C-T-F-E pays off most: you've stacked role, context, task, format, and now examples, each fixing a different failure mode.

options.label: Build a 47-variant A/B test of phrasing tweaks.
options.explain: Lernsy. Read the field notes again.

options.label: Fine-tune a model on prior emails.
options.explain: Massive overkill for a quarterly artefact. Few-shot in the prompt is two minutes of work; fine-tuning is a project. Use the smaller hammer.

options.label: Ship and let the legal team rewrite the awkward ones.
options.explain: You're externalising the cost to legal, who already hate this kind of thing. Two-line prompt fix vs ongoing legal time, this is not close.

outcomes.perfect: You shipped a working draft in 90 minutes by climbing R-C-T-F-E in order: role, context, format, examples. Riya is delighted. Ankit, on landing, sees the demo and Slacks: 'This is the discipline I want on every prompt we ship.'
outcomes.good: You got most of the levers in roughly the right order. The output is shippable with light legal edits. Re-read the cargo-cult section so you don't reach for chain-of-thought as a default.
outcomes.learn: You spent the 90 minutes adding 'think step by step' and tweaking temperature. The output is still generic. Re-read the lesson and try the battle again, this time forcing yourself to name which letter of R-C-T-F-E you are pulling at every step.

points: Prompts are an API — Role + Context + Task + Format + Examples
Examples are the dominant lever for structured tasks; 1-3 well-chosen examples beat all other tricks
One BAD example showing what to avoid is often more useful than a second good example
Cargo-cult phrases ('think step by step', tipping threats) move quality 0-5%; not the lever
Politeness has zero effect on quality; specifications have all the effect

lessons.title: The Hallucination Problem
lessons.subtitle: Why LLMs confidently lie, and what to actually do about it

audioChapters.label: Opening — confident liars and the cost of being wrong
Mental model: why hallucination is structural, not a bug
Move 1 — RAG (retrieval) as the real fix
Move 2 — When the cost of being wrong is too high to ship at all
Try it + reflect

blocks.md:
Hallucination is the biggest reason 'AI features' get rolled back. The model writes a plausible-sounding citation that doesn't exist. It generates a fictional case law. It invents an API endpoint. The output looks correct; verification is expensive; users notice.

By the end of this lesson, you'll have a model for *why* this happens (it's structural, not a bug), the canonical fix (RAG), and the judgment to refuse the use case when the cost of being wrong is too high.

blocks.title: Mental model: why hallucination is structural, not a bug
blocks.md:
Hallucination is not a temporary defect. It's a direct consequence of how LLMs work.

- The model produces the *most probable* continuation of a prompt.
- 'Most probable' and 'true' overlap most of the time but not always.
- The model has no internal mechanism to verify truth — only patterns of how true-sounding text *looks*.

So when you ask 'cite three Indian Supreme Court rulings on data-protection liability', the model produces three plausible-sounding citations. Some may be real. Some are likely fictional but follow the citation pattern perfectly.

**Hallucination is what happens when the model's confidence in pattern is interpreted as confidence in fact.** That interpretation is yours, not the model's.

hi-IN.title: Hostel ka 'topper' jo har question ka answer deta tha
hi-IN.md:
Hostel mein ek topper hota tha. Tu kuch bhi pucho — confident jawab. Last 4 ranks UPSC ke kaunsa? — *"Aman Sharma, Pranav Goyal, Kavya Iyer, Aditya Singh"*. Bhai impressed.

Fir tu ne Google kara — sab fake names. Topper ne *probable Indian names* aur *probable order* generate kara. Confidence high; truth zero.

**LLM bilkul same.** Pattern recognize karta hai 'list of 4 Indian names in formal context' — confidently produces. Verification chahiye toh **document reference do** — wo hai RAG. Naam invent nahi karega tab.

en.title: The hostel topper analogy
en.md: Every hostel had that one student who could answer any question with confident detail — half of which was made up. The model is the same. Without retrieval (RAG), it generates plausible patterns. With retrieval, it cites real documents. Confidence is identical in both cases; truth diverges.

blocks.text: Move 1 — RAG (retrieval) as the real fix

blocks.md:
**RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation.** The pattern: when a query needs factual grounding, *retrieve* the relevant documents first, then *pass them to the model* in the context, then *ask the model to answer using only those documents*.

In practice:

1. Embed the user's query into a vector.
2. Find the top-K most-similar document chunks from your corpus (vector DB).
3. Stuff those chunks into the prompt with explicit instructions: 'Answer using only the provided documents. If the answer is not in the documents, say so.'
4. Return the answer with citations to the chunks.

This pattern flips the failure mode. Without RAG, the model invents plausible facts. With RAG, the model either cites a real document or admits it doesn't know — both useful outcomes.

**RAG with citations is not optional for any AI feature in a regulated domain.** Legal, medical, financial, compliance — RAG is the price of admission.

steps.label: 1. User asks
steps.body: Query: 'What does the latest RBI circular say about UPI merchant fees?'

steps.label: 2. Without RAG
steps.body: Model produces: 'RBI Circular Ref. No. RBI/2024-25/47 dated June 12, 2024 states that...' — fabricated reference number. Plausible. False. Bad day for whoever cites it.

steps.label: 3. With RAG — embed
steps.body: User query is embedded into a vector. Vector DB indexed against the actual RBI circulars corpus.

steps.label: 4. With RAG — retrieve
steps.body: Top 3 chunks come back: actual RBI circular text from circular #DPSS.CO.PD.No.1093/02.14.003/2024-25 dated April 17, 2024.

steps.label: 5. With RAG — answer
steps.body: Model produces: 'Per RBI Circular DPSS.CO.PD.No.1093/02.14.003/2024-25 (April 17, 2024), Section 3, the merchant discount rate for UPI transactions remains zero for transactions up to ₹2,000.' Real citation. Real text. Grounded.
steps.code:
Prompt template:
  Given these documents:
  [chunk 1]
  [chunk 2]
  [chunk 3]
  Answer the user's question using only the documents.
  Cite sources by chunk ID. If unanswerable, say so.

blocks.prompt: What does RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) primarily fix?

choices.label: Hallucinated facts and citations — by grounding answers in retrieved documents and forcing the model to cite
choices.explain: Correct. RAG is the canonical fix for hallucination in domains where factual grounding matters.

choices.label: Latency
choices.explain: RAG adds a retrieval step; usually slower, not faster.

choices.label: Token cost
choices.explain: RAG typically increases token usage (you're stuffing chunks into the prompt). Cost is a tradeoff, not a fix.

choices.label: The model's intrinsic reasoning ability
choices.explain: RAG provides facts; reasoning quality depends on the model itself.

hi-IN.title: Bhabhi-ji ki recipe vs cookbook ka recipe
hi-IN.md:
Tu ne dal makhani banayi. Bhabhi-ji ko bhej ke pucha — *"recipe sahi hai?"* Bhabhi-ji ne phone pe bola — *"haldi 1 chamach, kasoori methi 2 chamach."*

Real cookbook (RAG): *"haldi half teaspoon, kasoori methi crushed 1 tablespoon."*

Bhabhi-ji ka jawab plausible tha. Cookbook ka jawab grounded hai. **Tu kis pe trust karega when stakes high?** Catering ka order ho toh cookbook. Casual dinner ho toh Bhabhi-ji bhi chalti hai.

**Same with LLM. Stakes decide whether you need RAG or not.**

en.title: When stakes decide retrieval
en.md: A family member's recipe-from-memory works for a casual dinner. A cookbook recipe is what you reach for when catering for 50 people. Same input, same outcome ~80% of the time, very different failure modes. Stakes decide which one you need.

blocks.text: Move 2 — When the cost of being wrong is too high to ship at all

blocks.md:
RAG fixes a lot. It does not fix everything. Some use cases should not be shipped with AI at all, regardless of how careful the engineering is.

**Refuse the use case when:**

- *The cost of being wrong is unbounded* (medical, legal, life-safety, regulatory non-compliance with civil penalties).
- *Verification is as expensive as doing it from scratch* (you'd have to re-do the work to check the AI's work — net negative).
- *Users cannot detect the failure mode* (a confident wrong answer to a question they don't have expertise to verify).
- *The deployment is unsupervised at scale* (1M users see the output before you spot a bad sample).

The ROI on saying 'no' to one of these is enormous. Most rolled-back AI features were rolled back because someone saw an upside without doing the math on the downside.

coach.name: RAG-Bhai Rohit
coach.role: Has rolled back 2 high-profile AI features

intro: Tell me — *ship with RAG*, *human-in-the-loop required*, or *refuse the use case entirely*?
I have scars from each category.

scenarios.situation: Internal docs Q&A bot for a mid-size SaaS company, answering employee questions about HR policies.
scenarios.explain: Classic RAG fit. Documents are well-defined (HR handbook), users can spot wrong answers (it's their own policy), stakes are bounded (worst case: HR clarifies).

scenarios.situation: AI auto-drafts surgery consent forms for hospitals based on the patient's procedure code.
scenarios.explain: Refuse. Cost of error: unbounded (legal liability, patient harm). Even with RAG, a confidently wrong consent paragraph could land a hospital in court. Use AI to *suggest* sections to a human-drafted form; never as the final author.

scenarios.situation: AI summarizes Indian Supreme Court rulings for a paid legal-research product, with citations to the actual ruling text.
scenarios.explain: Ship with RAG + lawyer review of the summary before publishing to paying customers. Without lawyer review, the citation might be real but the summary may misrepresent — high-stakes domain, paying customers, regulatory implications.

scenarios.situation: Auto-translate a meditation-app's daily-prompt content from English to 5 Indian languages.
scenarios.explain: Ship with native-speaker review for the first 100 prompts; once the eval-pass-rate is >95%, can move to spot-checks. Cultural nuances in spiritual-practice language are exactly where AI translations stumble; the cost of one bad translation is annoyance + churn.

scenarios.situation: Personal-finance Q&A chatbot answering 'should I invest in this fund?' for retail customers, citing past performance.
scenarios.explain: Refuse. SEBI regulations around investment advice apply; AI giving fund-specific advice is asking for a regulatory action. Rebrand to 'investor education' (general principles, no specific recommendations), or hire SEBI-registered advisors and build a different product.

blocks.title: The classic trap: the 'confident liar' shipped to customers
blocks.md:
Most rolled-back AI features have the same shape: launched without RAG (or with bad retrieval), confident outputs, mostly correct, occasional egregious failure. The egregious failures get screenshotted, posted on Twitter, the team rolls back.

The fix isn't tighter prompting. The fix is one of:

1. **Add RAG** — ground the output in real documents.
2. **Add human review** — the AI drafts, the human ships.
3. **Refuse the use case** — the cost of being wrong is too high.

Most teams reach for prompt tweaks because they're cheaper. Prompt tweaks are not the fix when the failure mode is hallucination; they're polish on a structural defect.

blocks.prompt: You're scoping an AI feature. Order these design questions from most-important to least:

items.label: What's the cost of a confident wrong answer? (unbounded → refuse; bounded → continue)
items.detail: First gate. If unbounded, no design fixes this.

items.label: Can the user detect a wrong answer? (no → human review or refuse; yes → can ship)
items.detail: Second gate. Detection determines whether scale is OK.

items.label: Do we have authoritative documents to ground in? (yes → RAG; no → no factual claims)
items.detail: Third gate. RAG is the workhorse for 'mostly factual' use cases.

items.label: Can we run an eval before launch? (yes → ship; no → don't ship yet)
items.detail: Fourth gate. No eval, no launch.

blocks.instruction: Pick one AI use case being considered at your work or in a side project. Write a 4-line refusal/acceptance memo: (1) cost-of-error bound, (2) user-detection ability, (3) RAG availability, (4) decision (ship / HITL / refuse).
blocks.expected:
Example use case: 'AI summarizes our internal Slack channels into a daily digest for the leadership team.'

(1) Cost-of-error: bounded. Worst case: a slightly inaccurate digest. Easily corrected by the human author the next day.
(2) User-detection: high. Leadership team is in the channels themselves; they spot inaccuracies immediately.
(3) RAG availability: not strictly required — the input is already the source. Could pass channel content directly into the prompt; no separate vector DB needed.
(4) Decision: SHIP, with a 1-week eval. If 90%+ digests need no correction, full launch. If not, add human-review step.

blocks.prompt: Pick the TWO TRUE statements about hallucination and RAG:

choices.label: Hallucination is structural — a consequence of next-token prediction without ground-truth verification
choices.explain: Correct. Not a bug to fix in the model; a property to engineer around.

choices.label: RAG is the canonical fix when factual grounding matters — retrieve documents, then generate with citations
choices.explain: Correct. Adds a real-data anchor before the model produces text.

choices.label: Tighter prompting alone fixes hallucination
choices.explain: False. Prompt tweaks reduce some hallucination but cannot fix the structural cause; only retrieval grounds the model in real documents.

choices.label: RAG is optional in regulated domains (legal, medical, financial)
choices.explain: False. RAG with citations is the price of admission for regulated-domain features.

hi-IN.title: Doctor-Aunty's classic — diagnosis vs Google
hi-IN.md:
Beta has fever. Tu Google kiya — *"could be malaria, dengue, typhoid, viral, COVID..."*. Kuch bhi possibility hai.

Doctor-Aunty ne pucha — *"kab se? body ache? rash? travel history? appetite?"* Specific symptoms ke saath, narrows down. **RAG vs no RAG ka real-life version.**

Google = LLM without retrieval, generic possibilities. Doctor = LLM with patient-specific retrieval, grounded answer. **Cost of error decides which one tu use karta hai.**

en.title: The diagnosis analogy
en.md: Googling symptoms gives you generic possibilities. A doctor with patient-specific retrieval (history, exam, labs) gives you a grounded answer. Same model of information, two very different fits. The cost of being wrong picks which one you use.

blocks.title: Field Notes: The Section Number That Did Not Exist
blocks.source: Anonymous, compliance lead at a Pune-based NBFC
blocks.story:
**Arundhati Capital**, a mid-sized Pune NBFC, had quietly rolled out an internal Slack bot that summarised RBI circulars for the credit-policy team. The bot was wrapping a frontier model with no retrieval layer; the team had pasted in 'recent circulars' as context once, then never updated.

In October 2025, an analyst asked the bot to summarise the *latest* RBI circular on digital lending fair-practice norms. The bot produced a confident, well-structured 4-paragraph summary. It cited **'Section 4.2(b) of RBI/2025-26/87'** as the source for a specific provisioning requirement. The analyst pasted the summary into a memo for the credit committee. The credit committee tightened a policy based on it. Operations ran with the new policy for **41 days**.

During legal review for an unrelated audit, an external counsel flagged the citation. The circular existed. The section did not. The provisioning requirement was a hallucination, plausible-sounding because the model had pattern-matched to the *style* of RBI circulars. The actual cost: a forced 6-week policy reversal, an internal investigation, a strongly-worded note from the board's risk committee, and **roughly 2.3 crore in foregone disbursements** during the over-tightened window.

The post-mortem identified the root cause in one line: **'No retrieval. No citations users could click. No grounding.'**
blocks.takeaway: In regulated domains, RAG with clickable citations is not optional. If a user cannot in two clicks verify the source of an AI claim, you have built a confident fiction generator wearing a compliance costume.

blocks.title: Architecting the Support Bot
blocks.setup: It is March 2026. The support-bot project from January is now your responsibility to architect. Velora's policies live in a versioned 80-page PDF (last updated 9 days ago) plus a Notion knowledge base of about 400 articles. Customers ask things like 'what is my interest rate if I prepay in month 4' and 'why was my loan rejected.' Ankit wants a recommendation by EOD.

stages.prompt: Three architectures on the table. Which do you take to Ankit?

options.label: **Ship now without RAG.** Just a strong system prompt that says 'only answer based on Velora policy.'
options.explain: This is Arundhati Capital. The model has no idea what Velora's policy is; the instruction 'only answer based on policy' will be cheerfully ignored because there is no policy in its context. You will hallucinate rates, terms, and rejection reasons in week one.

options.label: **RAG with mandatory citations** for every factual claim, sourced from the versioned PDF and Notion KB. Refuse to answer if retrieval returns nothing relevant.
options.explain: Correct. RAG is non-optional in regulated domains. Mandatory citations let customers and your own QA team verify every answer in one click. The 'refuse if retrieval is empty' rule is the load-bearing piece, it converts hallucinations into honest 'I don't know, here's a human' fallbacks.

options.label: **Refuse the use case entirely.** Hire more support staff.
options.explain: Over-conservative for a use case where the source-of-truth is *your own documented policies*. This is the canonical RAG sweet spot.

options.label: **Fine-tune** a model on the PDF and KB.
options.explain: Fine-tuning bakes in *today's* policies. The PDF was updated 9 days ago and will be updated again. You'd need to retrain every refresh, and customers would still get stale answers in between. RAG handles freshness for free.

stages.prompt: Ankit signs off on RAG. Now: what is the **single most important** failure mode you must engineer against on day one?

options.label: Latency. The bot must reply in under 2 seconds.
options.explain: Latency matters but a 4-second correct answer beats a 2-second hallucination every time. Wrong priority on a regulated bot.

options.label: **Retrieval-source mismatch:** the model answers using its pre-training knowledge instead of the retrieved chunks, even when chunks are present.
options.explain: This is the silent killer. The model 'helpfully' supplements retrieved context with its own training-data memory of how *most* fintechs work, and you ship a confidently wrong answer that looks grounded. Defences: explicit 'answer ONLY from CONTEXT, refuse otherwise' instruction, evals that test retrieval-blank cases, and a citation requirement so missing citations become a visible signal.

options.label: Cost. Tokens are expensive at 200K context.
options.explain: At roughly 3 dollars per million input tokens for a frontier model in 2026 and a typical retrieval payload of a few thousand tokens, your support-bot per-query cost is in single-digit rupees. This is not the hill.

options.label: Profanity in customer queries.
options.explain: Real but minor; off-the-shelf moderation handles it. Not the dominant failure mode of a RAG bot.

stages.prompt: Riya asks: 'What if the customer asks something the KB does not cover, like 'should I take this loan'?' How do you handle out-of-scope?

options.label: Refuse politely and route to a human agent. Never let the bot give financial advice.
options.explain: Correct, two reasons. One: 'should I take this loan' is investment advice, which in India requires registration the bot does not have. Two: out-of-scope refusal with handoff is the *only* way to keep the trust contract honest. The moment the bot pretends to know things outside its retrieval scope, you are back to Arundhati.

options.label: Let the model freelance with a disclaimer.
options.explain: Disclaimers do not protect you from SEBI's investment-advice rules. And a customer who got bad advice from your bot will not be mollified by small-print.

options.label: Train the bot to say 'definitely take it' to drive conversion.
options.explain: This is a regulator-bait answer wearing a growth-team costume. Do not.

options.label: Give a generic 'consult a financial advisor' response and end the chat.
options.explain: Half right. The 'consult an advisor' framing is fine but ending the chat without offering a Velora human is bad CX. The right pattern is refuse + offer handoff in the same turn.

stages.prompt: Last call: how do you measure that the RAG bot is *actually* not hallucinating, in production, week after week?

options.label: Trust customer NPS. If it drops, investigate.
options.explain: By the time NPS moves, you have already shipped weeks of bad answers. Lagging indicator. This is the workflow trap from Lesson 5 in miniature.

options.label: Eval set of 200 labelled questions, run nightly. Plus weekly sample-and-grade on 50 real production conversations. Plus a hard-flag rule: any response missing a citation is auto-escalated to QA.
options.explain: Three layers, three timescales. Eval set catches regressions on *known* cases. Sampled production grade catches drift on *new* cases. The citation hard-flag catches the dangerous failure mode (model bypassing retrieval) immediately. We will deepen this in Lesson 5.

options.label: Have one engineer skim the logs every Friday.
options.explain: Will not survive contact with reality. By month two no one is skimming. You need the eval set in CI and the citation flag in runtime.

options.label: Just count escalations to humans. Lower escalations is better.
options.explain: Perverse incentive. The bot will learn (via your prompt tweaks) to confidently *avoid* escalating, even when it should. Lower escalation can mean *more* hallucination, not less.

outcomes.perfect: You shipped a RAG architecture with mandatory citations, retrieval-only-answer enforcement, out-of-scope handoff, and a three-layer eval. Ankit forwards your design doc to the board with a one-liner: 'This is how we ship AI in regulated domains.' Velora's bot will go live in April with a clean trust surface.
outcomes.good: Most of the architecture is right. You may have under-weighted the retrieval-source-mismatch failure mode or the citation hard-flag. Re-read the hallucination-defences section and tighten the spec before build.
outcomes.learn: You shipped without retrieval, or trusted disclaimers, or relied on NPS. Read the Arundhati story again, then redo the battle. In regulated domains the cost of hallucination is not 'awkward,' it is 2.3 crore and a board memo.

points: Hallucination is structural — a property of next-token prediction, not a bug
Confidence and truth overlap most of the time and diverge on the dangerous edges
RAG (retrieval) is the canonical fix — ground answers in real documents, force citations
In regulated domains, RAG with citations is the price of admission, not optional
Some use cases should be refused regardless of engineering effort — when cost-of-error is unbounded

Picking the right AI use case is a more important skill than picking the right model. The features that ship and the features that get rolled back differ less in their engineering than in their initial framing.

By the end of this lesson, you'll have a 3-axis framework that lets you scope any candidate AI use case in 60 seconds and know whether to greenlight, scope for human-in-the-loop, or refuse.

blocks.title: Mental model: volume × stakes × verifiability
blocks.md:
Three axes pick whether AI fits a use case:

- **Volume** — how many decisions / outputs per day? More volume = more amortization of building cost; AI shines.
- **Stakes** — what's the cost of one wrong output? Bounded (annoyance, retry) vs unbounded (legal liability, patient harm).
- **Verifiability** — can the user or a downstream system detect a wrong output cheaply?

**Sweet spot: high volume + low stakes + high verifiability.** Customer-support ticket triage, summarization for spot-checking, internal docs Q&A.

**Never-ship zone: low volume + high stakes + low verifiability.** Drafting medical consent forms, generating final legal contracts, picking your team's annual strategy.

blocks.caption: Plot 5 candidate AI features on the 3-axis cube; watch them slot into ship / HITL / refuse zones.

hi-IN.title: Mummy ki cooking AI test — kahaan use karein, kahaan na karein
hi-IN.md:
Mummy ke kitchen mein two scenarios:

**Scenario 1**: 30 logon ka roti. Volume high, stakes low (ek roti jali toh OK), verifiability high (Mummy dekh leti hain). **AI assistant for roti-rolling? Sure, ship it.**

**Scenario 2**: Daadi-ji's birthday cake — recipe naani ne diya hai, single batch, 70 saal ka tradition. Volume low, stakes high, verifiability low (cake banane ke baad pata chalega galat hai). **AI assistant? Refuse. Mummy khud banayegi.**

**Same kitchen, same Mummy, alag fit.** Use case decides, not the tool.

en.title: Same kitchen, two fits
en.md: 30 rotis for a party: high-volume, low-stakes, easy to spot a bad one. Perfect for an AI assistant. Grandmother's birthday cake from a 70-year recipe: low-volume, high-stakes, no second chance. Refuse. The kitchen is the same; the use case decides.

blocks.text: Move 1 — High-volume + low-stakes is the sweet spot

blocks.md:
Most successful production AI features sit in the same corner: high-volume, low-stakes, high-verifiability.

Why: at high volume, you can afford to build infra, evals, and monitoring. Low stakes mean a wrong answer doesn't cost much. High verifiability means you catch failures before they compound.

Examples that fit this corner:
- Customer-support ticket triage (1000s/day, low individual stake, support agent can fix)
- Code completion in IDEs (millions of completions/day, low stake per completion, developer can reject)
- Spam detection (millions of emails/day, occasional false positive easy to recover from)
- Search-result ranking (billions of queries, ranking can be re-clicked)
- Auto-tagging photos (billions of uploads, wrong tag is mild annoyance)

**The pattern: AI is generating drafts, suggestions, or first-pass classifications — the human or the system has the final say.**
